prompt:
Traffic congestion is becoming a serious problem in many large cities around the world.

What problems does heavy traffic cause? What can be done to reduce it?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Explain the problems caused by heavy traffic (economic, environmental, health, quality of life)
Suggest practical measures to reduce congestion
Explain how each measure would work
Support ideas with examples
Answer BOTH questions with balanced development

for: Problem: lost working hours and higher costs for businesses and deliveries
Problem: air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions harm health and the climate
Problem: stress, noise and less time for family and leisure
Problem: emergency vehicles are delayed
against: Solution: invest in fast, frequent and affordable public transport
Solution: congestion charges for driving into city centres (e.g. London, Stockholm)
Solution: safe cycle lanes and pedestrian-friendly streets
Solution: flexible working hours and remote work to spread peak demand

models.text:
In cities from Jakarta to Los Angeles, commuters routinely spend hours each week sitting in stationary traffic. This congestion imposes heavy costs on the economy, public health and quality of life, yet experience from several cities shows that it can be significantly reduced through a mixture of investment and pricing.

The economic consequences are perhaps the easiest to measure. When employees arrive late and delivery vans move at walking pace, businesses lose productive time and their costs rise, which is eventually passed on to consumers in higher prices. Congestion also damages health. Vehicles crawling through crowded streets emit more pollutants per kilometre than those moving freely, and prolonged exposure to these emissions has been linked to asthma and heart disease. Furthermore, long and unpredictable journeys increase stress and leave people with less time for their families, exercise and rest, while ambulances and fire engines may be delayed at critical moments.

The most effective long-term remedy is to give people an attractive alternative to the car. Metro and bus networks must be frequent, reliable and affordable; if public transport is slow or overcrowded, few drivers will switch to it. Many European cities have also shown that well-designed, segregated cycle lanes encourage large numbers of people to cycle to work, as in Copenhagen, where cycling now accounts for a substantial share of commuter journeys.

Alongside these improvements, governments can discourage unnecessary car use. Congestion charges, which require drivers to pay to enter the city centre at busy times, have reduced traffic noticeably in London and Stockholm, and the revenue can be reinvested in public transport. Employers can contribute too, by allowing flexible hours or remote work so that fewer people travel at the same peak times.

In conclusion, traffic congestion harms productivity, health and well-being. Combining better public transport and cycling infrastructure with sensible restrictions on driving offers the best chance of keeping cities moving.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): responde plenamente a las dos preguntas: problemas económicos, sanitarios y sociales bien explicados, y soluciones concretas organizadas en dos tipos (alternativas al coche y desincentivos). Ejemplos precisos (Copenhague, Londres, Estocolmo). Coherence & Cohesion (8): excelente organización; 'Alongside these improvements' y 'The most effective long-term remedy' muestran jerarquía de ideas. Lexical Resource (8): léxico temático rico ('stationary traffic', 'crawling', 'segregated cycle lanes', 'congestion charges', 'peak times', 'revenue'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): estructuras complejas (relativas no especificativas, condicionales, pasivas) usadas con precisión. Para un 9: alguna reflexión más crítica (p. ej., por qué ampliar carreteras no funciona: tráfico inducido) que demuestre un dominio aún mayor del tema.

models.text:
Nowadays, many big cities suffer from heavy traffic, especially during rush hour. This situation causes several serious problems, but there are also some effective solutions that governments and individuals can adopt.

To begin with, traffic jams waste a lot of time. People who drive to work may spend one or two hours a day in their cars, which means they have less time for their families and hobbies. This can also make them tired and stressed before they even start working. Another important problem is pollution. Thousands of cars produce harmful gases that make the air dirty and cause breathing problems, such as asthma, especially among children and elderly people. Finally, traffic is bad for the economy, because goods are delivered late and workers lose productive hours.

There are several ways to reduce traffic in cities. The most important solution is to improve public transport. If buses and trains are cheap, fast and comfortable, many people will leave their cars at home. For example, in Madrid the metro system is very efficient, so many residents do not need a car at all. In addition, governments could charge drivers a fee to enter the city centre, as London has done. This encourages people to use other forms of transport. Lastly, cities should build more cycle lanes, so that people can travel safely by bicycle, which is also good for their health.

In conclusion, traffic congestion leads to wasted time, pollution and economic losses. However, by improving public transport, charging drivers and promoting cycling, cities can reduce traffic and become better places to live.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): responde a ambas preguntas con ideas pertinentes y ejemplos (Madrid, Londres). Las soluciones están algo menos desarrolladas que los problemas (la tasa de congestión se explica en una sola frase). Coherence & Cohesion (7): estructura muy clara, con conectores correctos pero enumerativos ('To begin with', 'Another important problem', 'Finally', 'In addition', 'Lastly'). Lexical Resource (7): vocabulario adecuado ('rush hour', 'harmful gases', 'productive hours', 'cycle lanes'), con algunas expresiones simples ('make the air dirty', 'bad for the economy'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buen control de condicionales y relativas; sin errores relevantes. Para subir a 8: explicar mejor el mecanismo de cada solución (por qué funciona, qué condiciones necesita), sustituir expresiones generales por léxico preciso ('emissions', 'air quality') y variar la forma de enlazar.

prompt:
The amount of plastic waste produced around the world is increasing every year, and much of it ends up in the oceans.

What problems does this cause? What can individuals and governments do to address them?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Explain the problems caused by plastic waste (wildlife, food chain, health, economy)
Suggest what INDIVIDUALS can do
Suggest what GOVERNMENTS can do
Explain how the solutions would work, with examples
Answer every part of the question with balanced development

for: Problem: marine animals swallow plastic or become entangled and die
Problem: microplastics enter the food chain and may affect human health
Problem: plastic takes hundreds of years to break down, so damage accumulates
Problem: polluted beaches harm tourism and fishing
against: Individuals: carry reusable bags and bottles, refuse unnecessary packaging
Individuals: sort waste correctly and take part in clean-ups
Governments: ban or tax single-use plastics (bags, straws, cutlery)
Governments: make producers responsible for packaging; deposit-return schemes for bottles

models.text:
Plastic has become one of the defining materials of modern life, but its durability, the very quality that makes it useful, also makes it an environmental hazard. Millions of tonnes of plastic waste reach the oceans each year, causing a range of serious problems which can only be tackled through action by both individuals and governments.

The most visible damage is to marine life. Seabirds, turtles and whales frequently mistake plastic bags and fragments for food, and many die with stomachs full of material they cannot digest; others become entangled in discarded fishing nets. Less visible, but potentially more worrying, are microplastics: tiny particles produced as larger items break down. These are absorbed by plankton and fish and thus enter the human food chain, with long-term health effects that scientists are only beginning to understand. In addition, coastal communities suffer economically when beaches covered in rubbish deter tourists and fish stocks decline.

Individuals can make a meaningful contribution, particularly if their choices are multiplied across a population. Carrying reusable bags, bottles and coffee cups, avoiding heavily packaged products and sorting rubbish correctly all reduce the amount of plastic that escapes into the environment. Consumer pressure can also influence companies: several supermarket chains have introduced packaging-free sections in response to customer demand.

However, the scale of the problem means that government action is indispensable. Bans on single-use items such as straws, cutlery and plates, already introduced across the European Union, remove some of the most common forms of litter at a stroke. Deposit-return schemes, in which consumers pay a small refundable charge on each bottle, have achieved collection rates of over ninety per cent in countries such as Germany and Norway. Governments can also require manufacturers to take financial responsibility for recycling the packaging they produce, which encourages them to design products that use less plastic in the first place.

In conclusion, plastic pollution threatens wildlife, human health and local economies. While individual habits matter, decisive legislation is the key to reducing the flow of plastic into the sea.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): cubre las tres partes (problemas, individuos, gobiernos) con desarrollo completo y ejemplos concretos (UE, Alemania, Noruega); además establece una jerarquía razonada (la acción gubernamental es indispensable por la escala del problema). Coherence & Cohesion (8): progresión impecable; 'Less visible, but potentially more worrying', 'However, the scale of the problem means...' enlazan con naturalidad. Lexical Resource (8): léxico rico y exacto ('durability', 'entangled', 'microplastics', 'deter', 'at a stroke', 'deposit-return schemes', 'refundable charge'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): gran variedad (inversión 'Less visible... are microplastics', relativas, aposiciones) sin errores. Para un 9: algún matiz adicional (p. ej., el papel del reciclaje frente a la reducción) y una introducción algo más directa.

models.text:
Every year, people around the world produce more and more plastic waste, and a large part of it ends up in the sea. This causes several serious problems, but both individuals and governments can take action to reduce them.

The main problem is the damage to sea animals. Fish, turtles and birds often eat pieces of plastic because they think it is food, and they can die as a result. Other animals get trapped in plastic nets or bags. Another problem is that plastic breaks into very small pieces called microplastics, which are eaten by fish. When people eat these fish, the plastic enters our bodies, and this may be harmful to our health. Moreover, dirty beaches are bad for tourism, which is an important source of income in many coastal areas.

Individuals can help in several ways. Firstly, they can use reusable shopping bags and water bottles instead of buying new plastic ones every day. Secondly, they should recycle their rubbish correctly so that plastic does not go to landfill or into the sea. Some people also join volunteer groups that clean beaches at weekends.

However, governments have more power to change the situation. They can ban single-use plastic products, such as straws and plastic cutlery, as many European countries have already done. They can also make companies use less packaging or more environmentally friendly materials. Finally, governments could fund campaigns to educate people about the dangers of plastic pollution.

In conclusion, plastic waste harms animals, human health and the economy. If individuals change their habits and governments introduce strict laws, the amount of plastic in our oceans can be reduced significantly.

Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): estructuras complejas correctas (relativas, 'so that', condicional); errores casi inexistentes. Para subir a 8: desarrollar al menos una medida con detalle y evidencia (p. ej., sistemas de depósito y retorno), y emplear léxico más preciso ('entangled', 'deter tourists').

prompt:
In the past, many people stayed in the same job or with the same employer for their whole working life. Today, people change jobs and even careers several times.

What are the reasons for this change? What effects does it have on individuals and on society?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Explain the reasons (causes) why people change jobs and careers more often
Explain the effects on individuals
Explain the effects on society
Support ideas with explanation and examples
Answer both questions with balanced development

for: Cause: technology makes some jobs disappear and creates new ones
Cause: short-term contracts and less job security offered by employers
Cause: people expect personal fulfilment and work-life balance, not just a salary
Cause: online job platforms and retraining courses make moving easier
against: Effect: individuals gain varied skills and higher salaries, but face insecurity and stress
Effect: difficulty getting mortgages or planning a family without stable income
Effect: companies lose experienced staff and spend more on recruitment and training
Effect: a more flexible economy where skills move to growing industries

models.text:
The idea of a 'job for life', in which an employee joined a company after leaving school and retired from it forty years later, has largely disappeared. Workers today frequently move between employers and even retrain for entirely different professions. This shift has both economic and cultural causes, and its effects on individuals and society are decidedly mixed.

The most fundamental reason is technological change. Automation and digitalisation have eliminated many routine occupations, from bank clerks to factory workers, while creating demand for roles that did not exist a generation ago, such as data analysts or social media managers. Workers often have little choice but to adapt. At the same time, employers have become less willing to offer permanent contracts, preferring flexible arrangements that allow them to respond quickly to market conditions. Attitudes have also changed: younger workers in particular tend to regard a job as a source of personal fulfilment and are prepared to leave if they feel undervalued or bored.

For individuals, the consequences cut both ways. Changing jobs can bring higher salaries, a broader range of skills and greater satisfaction; someone who moves from teaching into educational software design, for instance, may find the combination of experience highly valued. On the other hand, the lack of security can be a heavy burden. Without a stable income, it is harder to obtain a mortgage, plan a family or save for retirement, and the constant need to compete for new positions is a source of considerable stress.

For society, high mobility allows labour to flow towards expanding industries, which helps the economy adapt. However, companies lose valuable knowledge when experienced staff leave, and they may be reluctant to invest in training workers who are unlikely to stay. Governments, meanwhile, face growing pressure to provide retraining programmes and to adapt pension and welfare systems designed for a world of lifelong employment.

In conclusion, frequent career change is driven by technology, employer strategies and new expectations of work. It brings opportunity and flexibility, but also insecurity that both individuals and institutions must learn to manage.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): responde a las dos preguntas y separa claramente efectos individuales y sociales, como pide el enunciado. Causas variadas (tecnología, empresas, actitudes) bien explicadas y ejemplos concretos (de profesor a diseño de software educativo). Coherence & Cohesion (8): estructura muy clara (causas, efectos individuales, efectos sociales); conectores integrados con naturalidad ('At the same time', 'cut both ways', 'meanwhile'). Lexical Resource (8): léxico preciso y natural ('job for life', 'routine occupations', 'undervalued', 'heavy burden', 'labour to flow', 'welfare systems'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): estructuras complejas variadas sin errores. Para un 9: aún más concisión en algún párrafo y un efecto social menos previsible (p. ej., sobre la vida comunitaria o la movilidad geográfica).

models.text:
In the past, it was normal for people to work for the same company for most of their lives. Nowadays, however, many people change their job or even their career several times. This essay will discuss the reasons for this trend and its effects on individuals and society.

There are several reasons why people change jobs more often today. Firstly, technology is changing the job market very quickly. Many traditional jobs, such as factory work, have been replaced by machines, so workers have to find new types of employment. Secondly, companies now offer more temporary contracts, which means that employees cannot expect to stay in one place for a long time. Finally, people's attitudes have changed. Young people want jobs that are interesting and give them a good work-life balance, and if they are not happy, they are more willing to leave.

This trend has both positive and negative effects on individuals. On the positive side, people can gain different skills and experiences, which may help them earn a higher salary. For example, my brother worked in three companies in five years, and each time his salary increased. On the negative side, changing jobs can cause stress and insecurity, especially when people do not know if they will have work in the future.

For society, the effects are also mixed. The economy can become more flexible because workers move to industries that need them. However, companies may spend a lot of money on training new employees who leave after a short time.

In conclusion, people change jobs more often because of technology, temporary contracts and new attitudes. This brings both opportunities and problems for individuals and society.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): cubre todas las partes con ideas relevantes; el ejemplo del hermano es concreto, aunque personal. El párrafo sobre la sociedad es breve y menos desarrollado. Coherence & Cohesion (7): estructura clara y lógica, con conectores correctos pero formulaicos ('Firstly', 'Secondly', 'Finally', 'On the positive side'). Lexical Resource (7): vocabulario adecuado ('temporary contracts', 'work-life balance', 'insecurity'), con algunas expresiones generales ('a lot of money', 'very quickly'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buen control (relativas, 'which means that', comparativos); 'worked in three companies' sería mejor 'worked for'. Para subir a 8: desarrollar más los efectos sociales (pérdida de experiencia, sistemas de pensiones), incluir consecuencias concretas de la inseguridad (hipotecas, planificar una familia) y variar la cohesión.

prompt:
In many developing countries, large numbers of people are moving from rural areas to cities.

Why is this happening? What effects does this have on both the countryside and the cities?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Explain why people are moving from rural areas to cities
Explain the effects on the countryside
Explain the effects on the cities
Support ideas with explanation and examples
Cover all three parts with reasonable balance

for: Cause: better-paid jobs in factories, construction and services
Cause: farming is mechanised or unprofitable; climate change damages harvests
Cause: better schools, hospitals and entertainment in cities
Cause: young people attracted by modern urban lifestyles seen in the media
against: Countryside: ageing populations, abandoned farms, closing schools and shops
Countryside: money sent home by migrants can improve family incomes
Cities: overcrowding, slums, pressure on housing, water and transport
Cities: a larger workforce drives economic growth

models.text:
Across Asia, Africa and Latin America, millions of people leave their villages every year in search of a new life in the city. This migration is driven by a combination of economic need and changing aspirations, and it is transforming both the places people leave and those to which they move.

The primary motive is economic. In many rural areas, farming provides a precarious living: plots are small, prices for crops are low and, increasingly, droughts and floods linked to climate change destroy entire harvests. Cities, by contrast, offer wage-earning jobs in construction, manufacturing and services that, though often poorly paid, are far more reliable. Access to services is another powerful attraction. Parents who want their children to attend a good secondary school or need regular medical treatment frequently have little choice but to move. Finally, for many young people, urban life simply represents opportunity and modernity, an image reinforced by television and social media.

The effects on the countryside are profound. Because it is mainly the young who leave, villages are left with ageing populations, and farms may be abandoned for lack of labour. As the population falls, schools, clinics and shops close, which in turn prompts further departures. On the other hand, migrants often send part of their earnings home, and these remittances can fund better housing and education for the relatives who remain.

For the cities, rapid growth brings both dynamism and strain. A large, young workforce fuels economic expansion, as the rise of manufacturing centres in southern China demonstrated. Yet urban infrastructure rarely keeps pace with arrivals. The result is often overcrowded informal settlements without adequate sanitation, roads choked with traffic and intense competition for housing and jobs, which can lead to unemployment and crime.

In conclusion, rural-urban migration is caused by the search for income, services and a modern lifestyle. While it supports urban economies and provides rural families with remittances, it also hollows out villages and places severe pressure on cities, so careful planning is needed in both.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): cubre las tres partes (causas, efectos rurales, efectos urbanos) con desarrollo equilibrado, matices (efectos positivos y negativos en ambos espacios) y ejemplos (sur de China). Coherence & Cohesion (8): estructura impecable con un párrafo por parte; la cadena causal ('which in turn prompts further departures') demuestra cohesión avanzada. Lexical Resource (8): vocabulario rico y preciso ('precarious living', 'remittances', 'informal settlements', 'sanitation', 'keeps pace with', 'hollows out'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): estructuras complejas y variadas (concesivas 'though often poorly paid', relativas, causales) sin errores. Para un 9: un ejemplo concreto también para el campo y una conclusión algo más precisa sobre qué tipo de planificación sería necesaria.

models.text:
In many developing countries, a growing number of people are leaving the countryside and moving to big cities. This essay will explain the main reasons for this trend and its effects on rural and urban areas.

The most important reason is employment. In rural areas, most people work in agriculture, which is hard work and often does not pay well. In cities, there are more job opportunities in factories, offices and shops, and salaries are usually higher. Another reason is the lack of services in the countryside. Many villages do not have good schools or hospitals, so families move to cities to give their children a better education and to receive better healthcare. In addition, many young people are attracted by the modern lifestyle of the city, with its shopping centres, restaurants and entertainment.

This migration has serious effects on the countryside. Since most of the people who leave are young, villages are left with mainly elderly residents. As a result, there are not enough workers for the farms, and some local businesses and schools have to close. However, some families benefit because their relatives in the city send them money.

Cities are also affected. When too many people arrive in a short time, there is not enough housing, so some people have to live in poor areas without clean water or electricity. Traffic and pollution also increase. For example, cities like Lagos and Dhaka have grown extremely fast, and they now face serious problems with overcrowding.

In conclusion, people move to cities mainly for jobs and better services. This causes an ageing population in rural areas and overcrowding in cities, so governments need to invest in both.

Lexical Resource (7): vocabulario adecuado ('agriculture', 'elderly residents', 'ageing population', 'overcrowding'), con algunas expresiones simples ('hard work', 'poor areas'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buen control de estructuras complejas; errores prácticamente ausentes. Para subir a 8: incluir algún efecto positivo en las ciudades, desarrollar cadenas de causa-efecto más elaboradas y usar léxico más específico ('remittances', 'informal settlements', 'infrastructure').

models.text:
Nowadays in many poor countries, a lot of people leave the villages and go to live in the cities. There are many reasons for this and it has effects in the countryside and in the cities.

The main reason is the money. In the villages, people work in the fields and they earn very little money. In the city they can find a job in a factory or in a shop and earn more. Also in the cities there are more things like hospitals, universities and cinemas. The young people think that the life in the city is more interesting and more modern, so they don't want to stay in the village with their parents.

The effects in the countryside are negative. Only old people stay in the villages and there is nobody to work in the fields. Some villages become empty and the houses are abandon. Also the schools close because there are not enough children.

The effects in the cities are also negative. There are too many people and not enough houses, so the prices of the flats goes up. Some people have to live in very bad conditions without water or electricity. Also there is more traffic, more pollution and more crime because some people can not find a job. For example, in my country the capital city is very crowded and it is difficult to live there.

In conclusion, people move to the cities because they want more money and a better life. But this cause problems in the countryside and in the cities. The governments should create more jobs in the villages so people don't need to move.
models.commentary: Task Response (6): responde a las tres partes, pero todos los efectos se presentan como negativos sin matices, y las ideas son generales; la solución final (crear empleo rural) no se pide en el enunciado. Coherence & Cohesion (6): estructura correcta con un párrafo por parte, pero con conectores repetitivos ('Also' en casi cada párrafo) y frases que se suceden sin relación explícita. Lexical Resource (6): vocabulario básico ('the money', 'more things', 'very bad conditions'); 'effects in' debería ser 'effects on'. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (6): errores frecuentes: 'the houses are abandon' (abandoned), 'the prices of the flats goes up', 'this cause', artículos innecesarios ('the money', 'the life in the city'). Para subir a 7: incluir algún efecto positivo (remesas, crecimiento económico) para mostrar un análisis equilibrado, eliminar ideas no pedidas y revisar participios y concordancia.

prompt:
Many people, especially young people, now read far fewer books than previous generations did.

What are the causes of this? What effects might this have on individuals and on society?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
checklist: Explain the causes of the decline in book reading
Explain the possible effects on individuals
Explain the possible effects on society
Support ideas with explanation and examples
Answer both questions with balanced development

for: Cause: smartphones, social media and streaming compete for leisure time
Cause: short-form content trains people to expect quick rewards, reducing patience for long texts
Cause: heavy study and work schedules leave little free time
Cause: fewer adults reading at home, so children lack role models
against: Effect: weaker vocabulary, concentration and writing skills
Effect: less empathy and imagination, which fiction helps develop
Effect: a less informed public, more vulnerable to simplified or false information
Effect: bookshops and libraries close; publishing industry changes

models.text:
Surveys in many countries indicate that the proportion of people who regularly read books, particularly for pleasure, has fallen considerably over recent decades, and the decline is steepest among teenagers. This trend can be explained largely by the rise of digital entertainment, and it has potentially serious consequences for both individuals and society.

The most obvious cause is competition for leisure time. A teenager with a smartphone has instant access to video platforms, games and social networks, all of which are designed to be as engaging as possible. Compared with these, a novel demands sustained effort before it offers any reward. Moreover, constant exposure to short-form content appears to shape habits of attention: people who are used to switching between fifteen-second clips may find it genuinely difficult to concentrate on a long text. A further factor is the example set at home. Children whose parents rarely read are far less likely to develop the habit themselves, and busy adults who spend their evenings on screens unintentionally pass this pattern on.

For individuals, reading less may have a measurable impact on language and thinking. Books expose readers to a wider and more sophisticated vocabulary than everyday conversation or online posts, and regular readers tend to write more fluently as a result. Research also suggests that reading fiction strengthens empathy, since it requires readers to imagine the thoughts and feelings of people very different from themselves.

The effects on society could be equally significant. A democracy depends on citizens who can follow complex arguments and evaluate evidence, skills that are developed through extended reading rather than through headlines and slogans. If these abilities weaken, people may become more susceptible to misinformation and simplistic political messages. Culturally, too, the closure of bookshops and local libraries would deprive communities of important shared spaces.

In conclusion, the decline in reading is driven mainly by digital distractions and changing habits of attention. Since it may weaken language skills, empathy and informed public debate, schools and families should make deliberate efforts to keep reading alive.
models.commentary: Task Response (8): responde con claridad a ambas preguntas y distingue efectos individuales y sociales; las causas son variadas (competencia por el ocio, hábitos de atención, ejemplo familiar) y bien explicadas. Usa modales prudentes ('may', 'could', 'appears to') adecuados para efectos 'possible'. Coherence & Cohesion (8): progresión clara; 'Compared with these', 'A further factor', 'Culturally, too' enlazan con naturalidad. Lexical Resource (8): léxico preciso y académico ('sustained effort', 'short-form content', 'susceptible to misinformation', 'deprive communities'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (8): gran variedad estructural (comparativas, relativas, condicional, 'all of which') sin errores. Para un 9: algún matiz adicional (p. ej., que se lee mucho texto en pantalla, aunque no libros) que muestre una comprensión aún más completa del fenómeno.

models.text:
These days, many people, particularly teenagers, read much less than their parents and grandparents did. There are several reasons for this change, and it may have negative effects on both individuals and society.

The main cause is technology. Smartphones, video games and streaming services offer entertainment that is fast, easy and always available. For many young people, watching a series on Netflix or scrolling through social media is more attractive than reading a book, which requires more time and concentration. Another cause is that people are busier than before. Students have a lot of homework and extra classes, while adults often work long hours, so they feel too tired to read in their free time. Furthermore, if parents do not read at home, their children are unlikely to see reading as an enjoyable activity.

This trend can have several effects on individuals. People who read less usually have a smaller vocabulary and may find it more difficult to express their ideas in writing. In addition, reading helps people to concentrate for long periods, so those who rarely read may have a shorter attention span. Reading novels also develops imagination and helps us understand other people's feelings.

As for society, a population that reads less might be less well informed. If people only read short news on social media, they may not understand complex issues, and they may believe fake news more easily. Moreover, bookshops and libraries may close because fewer people use them.

In conclusion, people read fewer books mainly because of technology and busy lifestyles. This could reduce people's language skills and concentration, and make society less informed, so it is important to encourage reading from an early age.
models.commentary: Task Response (7): cubre todas las partes con ideas relevantes; algunos efectos se mencionan sin desarrollo (la imaginación y la empatía en una sola frase). Coherence & Cohesion (7): organización clara; conectores correctos pero algo previsibles ('Another cause', 'Furthermore', 'In addition', 'As for society', 'Moreover'). Lexical Resource (7): vocabulario adecuado ('streaming services', 'scrolling', 'attention span', 'fake news'), con algunas expresiones simples ('more attractive', 'short news'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy (7): buen control de comparativas y condicionales; sin errores relevantes. Para subir a 8: desarrollar cada efecto con un paso más de explicación o evidencia, explicar por qué el contenido breve afecta a la atención y usar léxico más preciso ('misinformation', 'sustained concentration').

models.text:
Nowadays, the young people don't read books like in the past. They prefer to use the mobile phone and the internet. In this essay I will explain the causes of this situation and the effects for the people and the society.

The first cause is the technology. Today everybody have a smartphone and there are many apps like Instagram and TikTok. The young people spend many hours watching videos and they don't have time for read. Also the videos are more fun and more easy than the books, because you don't need to think a lot.

The second cause is that the books are expensive. A new book can cost twenty euros and the students don't have much money. On the internet everything is free, so they prefer to use it.

The effects of this are negative. If people don't read, they don't learn new words and their writing is worst. For example, many students make a lot of spelling mistakes in their exams because they never read. Also, reading is good for the imagination and the creativity, and without books the children are less creative.

For the society, it is also a problem. The people who don't read don't know about history and culture, and they believe everything they see on the internet. This is dangerous because there is a lot of fake news. Also the libraries are empty and some of them will close.

In conclusion, the young people read less because of the technology and because books are expensive. This is bad for them and for the society, so the parents and the schools should encourage the children to read more.
models.commentary: Task Response (6): responde a ambas preguntas con ideas relevantes, pero generales y a veces exageradas ('they believe everything they see on the internet'); la causa del precio de los libros es poco convincente sin mencionar las bibliotecas. Coherence & Cohesion (6): estructura clara pero mecánica ('The first cause', 'The second cause', 'Also' repetido). Lexical Resource (6): vocabulario básico ('more fun', 'bad for them', 'a lot'); falta léxico preciso sobre atención o comprensión. Grammatical Range & Accuracy (6): errores frecuentes: 'everybody have', 'time for read' (to read), 'more easy', 'worst' (worse), uso sistemático de 'the' con sentido general ('the young people', 'the technology', 'the society'). Para subir a 7: matizar las afirmaciones absolutas, desarrollar cada causa y efecto con una explicación más elaborada, y corregir artículos y comparativos.
